abstract: This paper examines online firestorms as complex collective phenomena that can arise from diverse sociological and technical processes despite appearing superficially similar. It uses the case of a pro-Vietnam firestorm targeting the Facebook 'digital embassy' of China in Italy during the COVID-19 pandemic to argue that firestorms should be understood not only as marketing-related reputational crises but also as forms of coordinated political digital protest. The study broadens conceptual understanding of online collective behavior by revealing the multiple underlying dynamics behind such events.
key_claims: Seemingly similar online collective behaviors, such as firestorms, can be driven by fundamentally different sociological and techno-communicative processes.
Online firestorms should not be conceived solely as marketing-related reputational crises, but also as coordinated political digital protests.
Understanding the underlying dynamics of firestorms reveals their multifaceted nuances rather than treating them as a uniform phenomenon.
methods: Case study of a specific online firestorm: a pro-Vietnam attack on the Facebook page (digital embassy) of China in Italy during the pandemic
Analysis of online collective behavior on Facebook (further methodological detail not available from the abstract)
findings: The examined firestorm functioned as a coordinated political digital protest rather than a conventional marketing reputational crisis (further specific findings not available from the abstract)
contributions: Expands the dominant marketing-oriented perspective on online firestorms to include political digital protest as a driver
Highlights the multiple sociological and techno-communicative processes that can underlie collective online behaviors
Provides an empirical case linking geopolitical tensions (China, Vietnam, Italy) with online collective action during the pandemic
framing: The paper situates itself within the study of online collective behavior and digital protest, engaging with and challenging the prevailing marketing/reputational-crisis framing of online firestorms by reframing them through a sociological and political-communication lens.
